newsitem.title: HONG KONG: UN refugee chief leaves HK boatpeople saga unsolved.
newsitem.headline: UN refugee chief leaves HK boatpeople saga unsolved.

text.p: The head of the United Nations' agency for refugees left Hong Kong on Tuesday without giving any guarantee that thousands of Vietnamese boatpeople still stuck in the territory could all be sent home soon.

Officials had hoped the visit by Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), would help find ways to speed up repatriation of more than 5,000 Vietnamese languishing in the territory's camps and settle the bill for their care.
She toured the camps and met top officials, but the visit left little hope that the camps would be cleared before Britain hands Hong Kong back to Beijing on July 1 after 150 years of colonial rule.
China has told the departing British that the camps must be cleared before the handover.
On Monday Ogata told Tung Chee-hwa, who will be the territory's first chief executive after its return to China, that the world needed Hong Kong to continue providing a humanitarian sanctuary.
But she held out little hope that Hong Kong would get back the more than HK$1 billion (US$130 million) it has paid on behalf of the UNHCR for the upkeep of refugee camps and detention centres.
"I do not have any money," she said.

About 1,300 of the Vietnamese in Hong Kong are recognised as genuine refugees eligible for resettlement overseas, but many have crime or drugs records that make it hard to find any country willing to offer them a home.
Nearly 4,000 are regarded as economic migrants who must return to Vietnam but need clearance by Hanoi. Many are ethnic Chinese whom Hanoi has not recognised as its citizens.

Vietnam denied on Tuesday that it was going slow on repatriation and said it would only accept proven Vietnamese nationals. Some of the migrants are ethnic Chinese who fled Vietnam after a 1979 border war with China.

Ogata dismissed a charge by the Human Rights Watch Asia pressure group that conditions at Hong Kong detention centres were terrible and worsening. She said living conditions were not as bad as those she had seen for displaced persons in other parts of the world.
About 50 Vietnamese migrants staged rooftop protests on Tuesday to urge the government to re-screen them for refugee status while another 102 boatpeople were flown back to Hanoi.
The 5,000 or so Vietnamese migrants are the last of 200,000 who landed in Hong Kong after fleeing their homeland following the 1975 communist victory in the Vietnam War.
